phy_ocra.15.0.summary: **Irradiation** is exposing an object or person to nuclear radiation from a source **outside** it; the object does **not become radioactive**, and exposure stops when the source is removed or shielded. **Radioactive contamination** is the unwanted presence of **radioactive atoms on or inside** a material or person; because the atoms themselves have been transferred, the contaminated object **keeps emitting radiation** until the atoms decay or are removed. Understanding the difference, and the precautions for each, lets you explain the hazards of ionising radiation and why contamination is usually harder to deal with.

core.p: Alpha, beta and gamma radiation are all **ionising**: they can remove electrons from atoms in the cells of the body. Ionisation can **damage or kill cells** and can damage **DNA**, which may cause **mutations** and lead to **cancer**. Very high doses can cause radiation sickness and burns.
bullets: Ionisation of molecules in cells can **disrupt cell processes** or kill the cell.
Damage to **DNA** can cause cells to divide uncontrollably, leading to **cancer**.
Damage to sex cells may cause **mutations** passed on to offspring.
The risk increases with **dose**: larger exposure means greater chance of harm.
People can be exposed in two different ways: **irradiation** and **contamination**.

callouts.p: Exposure to radiation can happen by irradiation (radiation from an outside source) or by contamination (radioactive atoms get onto or into you).

core.p: **Irradiation** is when an object or person is **exposed to nuclear radiation** from a source that stays **outside** them. The radiation passes into or through the object, but no radioactive material is transferred.
bullets: The source is **separate from** the object being irradiated.
The irradiated object **does not become radioactive**.
Exposure **stops as soon as** the source is removed, switched off or shielded.
Examples: having an X-ray image taken; **gamma sterilisation** of surgical instruments or food; standing near a radioactive source; radiotherapy beams aimed at a tumour.
Most dangerous from outside are **beta and gamma**, because they penetrate the skin; alpha cannot get past the dead outer layer of skin.

callouts.p: Exposing an object or person to nuclear radiation from an external source, without the object itself becoming radioactive.
Food or equipment sterilised by gamma rays is irradiated, not contaminated, so it does not become radioactive and is safe to use.

core.p: **Radioactive contamination** is the **unwanted presence of radioactive atoms** (radioactive material) on or inside another material or person. Because the radioactive atoms are now part of, or stuck to, the object, it keeps emitting radiation.
bullets: The radioactive **atoms themselves** have been transferred.
The contaminated object or person **becomes a source** of radiation.
Radiation continues until the atoms **decay** or are **removed** (washed off, excreted), so the hazard can last a long time.
Contamination can be **external** (on skin, clothes or surfaces) or **internal** (swallowed, breathed in, or through a cut).

Examples: radioactive dust settling on clothing; breathing in **radon gas**; eating food contaminated after a nuclear accident such as **Chernobyl**; a radioactive tracer injected into a patient (deliberate internal contamination for a medical purpose).

callouts.p: The unwanted presence of materials containing radioactive atoms on or in other materials.

core.p: The key difference is **where the radioactive atoms are**. In irradiation they stay in the source outside; in contamination they have moved onto or into the object.
bullets: Irradiation: **radiation** reaches you; contamination: **radioactive material** reaches you.
Irradiation **ends** when you move away or the source is shielded; contamination **continues** wherever you go.
Contamination can **spread** to other people and objects; irradiation cannot.
Contamination is generally considered **more dangerous** because exposure is close up and long lasting.

core.p: The danger of contamination depends on the type of radiation and on whether the material is **outside or inside** the body. Internal contamination by an **alpha emitter** is the most dangerous situation.
bullets: Inside the body, **alpha** is the most harmful: it is **strongly ionising** and all its energy is absorbed by a small volume of nearby tissue.
Inside the body, **gamma** is the least harmful: most of it **passes out** of the body without ionising.
Outside the body (external contamination on skin), alpha is stopped by the **dead outer skin layer**, but beta and gamma can reach living cells.
**Radon** is a radioactive gas that emits alpha particles; breathing it in contaminates the lungs and increases the risk of lung cancer.
Internal contamination is very hard to remove: the body may only clear it slowly by **excretion**.

Internal contamination

callouts.p: Do not say 'alpha is the most dangerous'. Say alpha is most dangerous INSIDE the body and least dangerous OUTSIDE, and explain using ionising and penetrating power.

core.p: To reduce irradiation you must reduce the amount of radiation reaching the body from the outside source. The three main ideas are **shielding, distance and time**.
bullets: **Shielding**: put lead, concrete or thick barriers between the source and people; lead aprons for radiographers; lead-lined storage boxes.
**Distance**: keep as far from the source as possible; handle sources with **long tongs** held at arm's length.
**Time**: keep exposure time as **short** as possible; radiographers leave the room or stand behind a screen when taking X-rays.
Never point a source at anyone; return sources to storage immediately after use.
Workers wear **dosimeters (film badges)** to monitor the dose they receive.

core.p: To prevent contamination you must stop radioactive **material** getting onto or into people and objects. This means keeping sources **sealed** and providing **barriers** between people and radioactive substances.
bullets: Wear **gloves**, protective clothing and overshoes so material cannot reach the skin.
Wear **masks or breathing apparatus** to avoid inhaling radioactive dust or gas.
Keep sources in **sealed containers**; use sealed sources in schools.
Do **not eat, drink or smoke** near radioactive materials; cover cuts.
**Wash hands** thoroughly after handling; monitor hands and clothing with a detector.
Dispose of contaminated items as **radioactive waste**; ventilate homes in high-radon areas.
Decontaminate by **washing or removing** contaminated clothing and surfaces.

callouts.p: Gloves and masks prevent contamination; they do almost nothing against gamma irradiation. Lead screens reduce irradiation but do not stop contamination.

core.p: Contamination is usually harder to control than irradiation because you **cannot simply walk away** from the source: the source goes with you.
bullets: Exposure is **continuous** until the radioactive atoms decay or are removed.
The source is **very close** to (or inside) living cells, so even alpha can do damage.
Contamination can **spread** to food, water, other people and places.
A long **half-life** isotope can keep contaminating an area for years (for example, around Chernobyl and Fukushima).
Decontaminating land, buildings and people is **difficult and expensive**.

core.p: Exam questions often describe a situation and ask whether it is irradiation or contamination. Ask yourself: has radioactive material been transferred?
bullets: A patient has an **X-ray** taken: **irradiation**.
Fruit is sterilised with **gamma rays**: **irradiation** (fruit is not radioactive).
A worker gets radioactive dust **on their skin**: **external contamination**.
A family breathes in **radon gas** in their home: **internal contamination**.
A patient is injected with a **gamma-emitting tracer**: deliberate **internal contamination** (the patient becomes a source for a while).
A tumour is treated with an **external beam** of gamma rays: **irradiation**.
A pilot receives a higher dose from **cosmic rays**: **irradiation**.

core.p: Scientists study the effects of radiation on people and **publish their findings** so that other scientists can check them through **peer review**. This helps make conclusions about risk reliable and lets safety guidelines be based on evidence.
bullets: The **dose** of radiation received is measured in **sieverts (Sv)** (usually millisieverts, mSv).
Higher dose means **higher risk** of harm; risk is weighed against benefits (e.g. medical scans).
Results must be **shared and repeated** by others before being accepted.
Guidelines for workers and the public are set from this evidence and regularly reviewed.

callouts.p: Publishing and peer review allow other scientists to check findings, identify errors and confirm the risks of radiation before safety rules are set.

analogy.p: Irradiation is like standing in the light from a lamp: the light reaches you, but when you step away or close a curtain (shielding), it stops, and you do not start glowing yourself. Contamination is like getting glitter on your hands: the glitter itself has been transferred, it goes everywhere you go, you can spread it to other people, and it keeps sparkling until you wash it off. Where it breaks down: glitter does not fade on its own, but radioactive atoms do decay over time according to their half-life; and getting radioactive material inside your body is far harder to wash off than glitter on your hands.

mistakes.w: Irradiated food becomes radioactive.
mistakes.r: Irradiated objects do not become radioactive; only radiation passes through them, not radioactive atoms.

mistakes.w: Contamination is when you are exposed to radiation.
mistakes.r: Contamination is when radioactive atoms or material get onto or into an object or person.

mistakes.w: Alpha is always the most dangerous radiation.
mistakes.r: Alpha is most dangerous inside the body (contamination) but least dangerous outside, as skin stops it.

mistakes.w: Wearing gloves protects you from gamma irradiation.
mistakes.r: Gloves prevent contamination; gamma irradiation is reduced by lead shielding, distance and less time.

mistakes.w: When you move away from contamination, exposure stops.
mistakes.r: Contamination moves with you; exposure only stops when the radioactive atoms decay or are removed.

mistakes.w: Irradiation can spread from person to person.
mistakes.r: Irradiation cannot spread; contamination can spread because radioactive material is transferred.

mistakes.w: A lead apron stops contamination.
mistakes.r: A lead apron reduces irradiation; contamination is prevented by sealed sources, gloves and masks.

mistakes.w: Radiation damages cells by heating them.
mistakes.r: Radiation damages cells by ionisation, which can damage DNA and cause mutations or cancer.

exam.q: Compare irradiation and contamination. In your answer explain the hazards of alpha, beta and gamma sources in each case and describe precautions to reduce the risks.

Contamination: radioactive atoms on/in object; it becomes a source; continues until atoms decay/removed; can spread

worked.q: Model answer: Classify each as irradiation or contamination: (a) a dental X-ray; (b) radioactive dust from an accident lands on vegetables; (c) a tumour is treated with an external gamma beam.
steps: (a) X-rays come from a machine outside the patient; no radioactive atoms transferred: irradiation.
(b) Radioactive atoms are now on the vegetables, which become sources: contamination.
(c) The gamma source stays outside the body; the patient does not become radioactive: irradiation.

worked.q: Model answer: A worker spills a liquid containing an alpha emitter on his hand. Explain the risks and what he should do.
steps: This is external contamination: radioactive atoms are on his skin.
Alpha cannot penetrate the dead outer layer of skin, so the risk from outside is low.
But the atoms could be transferred to his mouth, a cut or food, causing internal contamination where alpha is highly ionising and very harmful.
He should wash the area thoroughly, remove contaminated clothing, have his hands monitored with a detector and dispose of waste safely.
worked.ans: Low hazard while on the skin, but a serious risk if it becomes internal; he must decontaminate immediately and be monitored.

worked.q: Applied example: Explain why surgical gloves sterilised with gamma radiation inside sealed packets stay sterile and are safe for surgeons to use.
steps: Gamma is highly penetrating, so it passes through the sealed packaging.
It kills bacteria on the gloves by ionising and damaging their cells.
The packet stays sealed, so no new bacteria can enter.
The gloves are irradiated, not contaminated, so they do not become radioactive.
worked.ans: Gamma penetrates the packet and kills microbes; the gloves are irradiated rather than contaminated, so they are sterile and not radioactive.

phy_ocra.15.1.summary: The **half-life** of a radioactive isotope controls how its hazard is spread out over time. An isotope with a **short half-life** has a very high activity, so it is intensely dangerous at first, but it decays away quickly and soon becomes safe. An isotope with a **long half-life** has a low activity, so the dose rate is small, but it stays radioactive (and hazardous) for a very long time, which is why long-lived waste must be stored safely for thousands of years. Grade 9 answers link half-life to activity, dose, time, the type of radiation and whether the material is outside or inside the body.

core.p: Radioactive decay is **random**: you cannot predict when one nucleus will decay, but for a large number of nuclei the fraction that decays in a given time is fixed. That lets us define a half-life.
bullets: The half-life is the same for every sample of a given isotope, whatever its size.
After 1 half-life, 1/2 of the unstable nuclei remain; after 2, 1/4; after 3, 1/8; after n half-lives, (1/2)^n remain.
The **activity** (decays per second, measured in **becquerels, Bq**) also halves every half-life.
Half-lives range from fractions of a second to billions of years, which is why hazards differ so much.

callouts.p: The time taken for half of the unstable nuclei in a sample to decay, or the time taken for the activity (or count rate) of a sample to fall to half its initial value.

core.p: Activity depends on how many nuclei there are and how likely each is to decay. A short half-life means each nucleus is very likely to decay soon, so for the **same number of nuclei** the activity is much higher.
bullets: Short half-life: nuclei decay quickly, so many decays per second means **high activity**.
Long half-life: nuclei decay slowly, so few decays per second means **low activity**.
Total number of decays eventually is the same (one per nucleus), but the short-lived sample packs them into a short time.
Higher activity means more ionising radiation per second, so a higher **dose rate** to anyone nearby.

callouts.p: Short half-life = intense hazard for a short time. Long half-life = weaker hazard for a long time.

core.p: Isotopes with short half-lives (seconds, hours or days) give out radiation very quickly, so being close to a fresh source can give a large dose in a short time.
bullets: **Very high initial activity**, so a high dose rate and high risk of cell damage or mutation if exposed.
The hazard drops rapidly: after 10 half-lives the activity is about 1/1000 of the start.
Waste can often be **stored until it has decayed** to a safe level and then disposed of.
Good for medical tracers because the patient is not left radioactive for long.

callouts.p: Mark schemes reward 'decays quickly so does not remain radioactive for long' rather than vague phrases like 'goes away'.

core.p: Isotopes with long half-lives (thousands to billions of years) have low activity, but they remain radioactive for longer than human lifetimes.
bullets: **Low activity**, so the dose rate at any moment is relatively small.
The material stays hazardous for **a very long time**, so the total exposure over years can be large.
If it **contaminates** land, water or food, the area stays contaminated for generations.
Nuclear waste containing long-lived isotopes must be sealed, buried deep underground and monitored for thousands of years.

callouts.t: Long half-life does not mean more dangerous
callouts.p: A long half-life is not automatically 'more dangerous'. It is less intense at any moment but dangerous for longer. Say which kind of danger you mean.

core.p: Exam questions often ask you to compare two isotopes. Organise your answer around activity, duration and what that means for handling and disposal.
bullets: Compare the activity (dose rate) at the start.
Compare how long the source stays hazardous.
Say what this means for storage, disposal or use.
Mention the type of radiation emitted as a second factor.

core.p: Half-life matters most when material gets somewhere it should not be. **Contamination** means radioactive atoms are on or inside something, so it keeps being exposed until the atoms decay or are removed.
bullets: **Irradiation** stops as soon as you move away from or shield the source, whatever its half-life.
With contamination the person keeps receiving a dose; a long half-life means this continues for years.
A short half-life contaminant decays quickly, so the contamination becomes harmless sooner.
Inside the body, the body may also remove some material naturally, but half-life still sets how long it is active.

callouts.p: Contamination plus long half-life = long-lasting hazard. This is the reason fallout and leaked waste are such serious problems.

core.p: Half-life tells you how fast the radiation is given out; the **type of radiation** tells you how damaging and how penetrating it is. Good answers combine both.
bullets: **Alpha**: most ionising but stopped by skin or paper, so most dangerous **inside** the body.
**Beta**: moderately ionising, stopped by a few mm of aluminium.
**Gamma**: weakly ionising but very penetrating, so dangerous from **outside** the body too.
A short half-life alpha emitter swallowed or breathed in gives a large dose to nearby cells very quickly.

core.h: Using half-life to work out when a source is safe
core.p: Because activity halves every half-life, you can predict how long it takes a source to fall to a safe level. This is how hospitals and power stations plan storage.
bullets: Keep halving the activity until it is at or below the safe value; count the half-lives.
Time = number of half-lives x half-life.
Activity after n half-lives = initial activity x (1/2)^n.
A sample never quite reaches zero, so we talk about falling to a **safe** or **background** level.

core.p: Spent fuel from nuclear power stations contains a mixture of isotopes. The short-lived ones make it very hot and highly active at first; the long-lived ones keep it hazardous for thousands of years.
bullets: Fresh waste is stored under water to cool and to let short half-life isotopes decay.
Long-lived waste is sealed (for example in glass or steel and concrete) and stored deep underground.
Storage sites must stay secure and dry for thousands of years so that the waste does not leak into **groundwater**.
Low-level waste with short half-lives can be stored until its activity falls, then disposed of.

callouts.t: Why waste is a long-term problem
callouts.p: It is the long half-life isotopes that make nuclear waste a problem for future generations, not the short-lived ones.

core.p: Scientists choose an isotope so that its half-life is long enough to do the job but short enough not to leave a lasting hazard.
bullets: **Medical tracer**: half-life of a few hours, long enough to take an image, short enough to leave the body's dose small.
**Smoke alarm** (alpha source): long half-life so it does not need replacing for many years; alpha is safe outside the body.
**Dating rocks or remains**: long half-life so that a measurable amount is still left after a long time.
**Industrial leak tracer**: short half-life so the pipe or ground does not stay contaminated.

callouts.p: For 'why is this half-life suitable?' give both sides: long enough to... and short enough to...

core.p: Hazard is about how likely and how severe harm is. Half-life is one factor; others include the dose, the type of radiation, where the material is and how long someone is exposed.
bullets: Risk increases with activity, time of exposure and closeness to the source.
Risk is reduced by shielding, distance, limiting time and preventing contamination (gloves, tongs, sealed sources).
Decisions about using radioactive materials weigh the benefit against the risk.
Scientists publish and peer review data on dose and risk so decisions are based on evidence.

callouts.p: A tiny sample of a short half-life isotope may still be less hazardous than a large amount of a long-lived one. Comparisons need the same number of nuclei or the given activities.

core.p: Level of response questions reward a structured comparison with linked reasons. Aim for at least three linked points for each isotope plus a justified conclusion.
bullets: State the half-life of each isotope and what it means for activity.
Link activity to dose rate and harm (ionisation damages cells and DNA).
Link half-life to how long the hazard lasts and to storage or disposal.
Bring in the type of radiation and whether the source is inside or outside the body.
Finish with a conclusion that answers the question asked.

analogy.p: A short half-life isotope is like a firework: it releases its energy in a brief, dazzling burst that is dangerous if you are close, but is soon over. A long half-life isotope is like a candle with the same amount of wax: it gives off only a little at any moment but keeps burning for a very long time, so you have to watch it for ages. The analogy breaks down because a firework or candle can be put out, whereas radioactive decay cannot be sped up, slowed or stopped by any physical or chemical change, and decay is random rather than steady burning.

terms.d: The time taken for half of the unstable nuclei in a sample to decay, or for the activity of the sample to halve.
The rate at which a source of unstable nuclei decays, measured in becquerels (Bq).
The unit of activity: one decay per second.
The number of decays recorded each second by a detector such as a Geiger-Muller tube.
The random process in which an unstable nucleus gives out radiation to become more stable.
It is impossible to predict when a particular nucleus will decay, only the probability.
Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
Radiation with enough energy to remove electrons from atoms, which can damage cells and DNA.
A measure of the harm caused by the radiation absorbed by the body (measured in sieverts).
The unwanted presence of radioactive atoms on or inside other materials or a person.
Exposure of an object to nuclear radiation from a source outside it; the object does not become radioactive.
Low-level radiation around us all the time from natural and man-made sources.
Unwanted radioactive material, for example spent fuel from nuclear power stations.
A radioactive isotope put into a system so its path can be followed with a detector.
A change in DNA that can be caused by ionising radiation and may lead to cancer.

mistakes.w: A long half-life isotope is more radioactive.
mistakes.r: A long half-life means a LOWER activity for the same number of nuclei, but the source stays radioactive for longer.

mistakes.w: After two half-lives the sample has completely decayed.
mistakes.r: After two half-lives one quarter of the original nuclei (and activity) remain; it never reaches zero.

mistakes.w: Half-life is half the time it takes for the sample to decay.
mistakes.r: Half-life is the time for half of the unstable nuclei to decay (or the activity to halve).

mistakes.w: Short half-life isotopes are safe.
mistakes.r: They are very hazardous at first because of their high activity, but the hazard lasts only a short time.

mistakes.w: Heating or burying waste makes it decay faster.
mistakes.r: Nothing changes the half-life; storage just keeps the waste isolated while it decays.

mistakes.w: Irradiated objects become radioactive and stay dangerous for the half-life.
mistakes.r: Irradiation does not make an object radioactive; half-life matters for contamination, where radioactive atoms are present.

mistakes.w: The waste is dangerous because it is radioactive.
mistakes.r: Explain why: it emits ionising radiation that damages cells, and long half-life isotopes keep doing so for thousands of years.

mistakes.w: Dividing the time by the half-life gives the fraction left.
mistakes.r: Time divided by half-life gives the NUMBER of half-lives n; the fraction left is (1/2)^n.

exam.q: Define the term half-life.
model: Time taken for half of the unstable nuclei to decay / for the activity to halve.
exam.tip: Say 'unstable nuclei' or 'activity', not 'half the atoms disappear'.

exam.q: Two samples contain the same number of nuclei. Sample A has a half-life of 6 hours and sample B has a half-life of 5000 years. Which has the higher activity? Explain.
model: Sample A.
Nuclei decay more quickly / more decays per second for a shorter half-life.
exam.tip: Activity is decays per second, so faster decay means more decays each second.

exam.q: Explain why waste containing isotopes with long half-lives must be stored for thousands of years.
model: Activity takes a very long time to fall to a safe level / stays radioactive for a long time.
Still emits ionising radiation that can damage cells / cause cancer.
exam.tip: Two marks need two ideas: duration and harm.

exam.q: A source has an activity of 1200 Bq and a half-life of 8 days. Calculate its activity after 24 days.
model: 24 / 8 = 3 half-lives.
exam.tip: Always find the number of half-lives first.

exam.q: Suggest why a medical tracer should have a half-life of a few hours rather than a few seconds.
model: Long enough for it to reach the organ and for a scan to be taken before it decays.
exam.tip: Link the half-life to the time needed for the job.

exam.q: Suggest why a medical tracer should not have a half-life of many years.
model: Patient would remain radioactive for a long time.
Longer exposure / larger total dose so greater risk of cell damage or cancer.
exam.tip: Mention both 'remains radioactive' and 'risk of harm'.

exam.q: Radioactive material from an accident contaminates farmland. Explain why the half-life of the material affects how long the land cannot be used.
model: Contamination means radioactive atoms remain in the soil/crops.
They keep emitting radiation until they decay.
Long half-life means activity stays high for a long time, so land unusable for longer (short half-life: safe sooner).
exam.tip: Use the word contamination and link it to the atoms decaying.

exam.q: A waste store must keep a sample until its activity falls from 6400 Bq to 100 Bq. The half-life is 30 years. How long must it be stored?
model: 6 half-lives.
6 x 30 = 180 years.
exam.tip: Count arrows, not numbers, to get the number of half-lives.

exam.q: A technician says 'isotopes with short half-lives are always safer to work with'. Evaluate this statement.
model: Short half-life means high activity so a large dose rate if close to fresh sample.
So more dangerous at first / need shielding, tongs, short exposure.
But activity falls quickly so hazard lasts only a short time / easy to store until safe.
Conclusion: not always safer; it depends on time since produced, amount, and type of radiation.
exam.tip: Evaluate means give both sides and a judgement.

exam.q: Isotope X is an alpha emitter with a half-life of 3 days. Isotope Y is a gamma emitter with a half-life of 30 years. Compare the hazards of the two isotopes if a person is contaminated by them and if a person is irradiated by them from outside the body.
model: X has high activity due to short half-life; Y has low activity.
Alpha highly ionising so X very harmful inside the body, e.g. swallowed or inhaled.
Alpha stopped by skin so X little hazard from outside the body.
Gamma penetrating so Y harmful from outside and inside the body.
X decays quickly so contamination hazard lasts only days to weeks.
Y stays active for decades so contamination by Y is a long-lasting hazard; needs removing / long storage.
Justified conclusion about which is more hazardous in each situation.
exam.tip: Plan a grid: inside/outside against X/Y, then write a sentence for each cell.

worked.q: A hospital stores waste with an initial activity of 4000 Bq. The isotope has a half-life of 6 hours. It can be disposed of when the activity is below 300 Bq. What is the minimum storage time?
steps: 250 Bq is the first value below 300 Bq, reached after 4 half-lives.
Time = 4 x 6 hours = 24 hours.
worked.ans: 24 hours (4 half-lives). The short half-life means the waste becomes safe in about a day.

worked.q: What fraction of a long-lived isotope (half-life 24 000 years) remains after 72 000 years, and what does this mean for storage?
steps: Number of half-lives n = 72 000 / 24 000 = 3.
Fraction left = (1/2)^3 = 1/8.
So the activity is still 1/8 of its original value after 72 000 years.
worked.ans: 1/8 remains. Even after tens of thousands of years the waste is still significantly radioactive, so it must be stored securely, for example deep underground, for an extremely long time.

worked.q: Model answer: Explain why a sample of an isotope with a half-life of 2 minutes is more dangerous to hold for 1 minute than a sample with the same number of nuclei and a half-life of 2 million years, but less of a long-term problem.
steps: Shorter half-life means nuclei decay faster, so the activity is far higher.
Higher activity means more ionising radiation each second, so a larger dose in that minute.
After about 20 minutes (10 half-lives) the short-lived sample has decayed to about 1/1000 of its activity.
The long-lived sample barely changes, so it remains a (low-level) hazard for millions of years.
worked.ans: The short half-life sample gives a much larger dose rate now but becomes safe quickly; the long half-life sample gives a small dose rate but stays hazardous for an extremely long time.

phy_ocra.15.2.summary: Nuclear radiation is used in medicine in two main ways: to **explore internal organs** (imaging with **tracers**) and to **control or destroy unwanted tissue** such as cancer (**radiotherapy**). Imaging uses a **gamma emitter** with a short half-life, because gamma rays pass out of the body to a gamma camera and the patient is not left radioactive for long. Treatment uses ionising radiation to kill cells, either from **external gamma beams** aimed at the tumour from several directions or from a **source placed inside the body** next to the tumour. Every use must be evaluated by weighing the medical benefit against the risk of damaging healthy cells.

core.h: Why radiation is useful in medicine
core.p: Nuclear radiation is **ionising**: it knocks electrons off atoms. This can damage or kill cells, which is dangerous, but the same effect can be aimed at cancer cells. Radiation can also be detected outside the body, so it can show what is happening inside without surgery.
bullets: Two uses on the spec: **exploring internal organs** (diagnosis) and **controlling or destroying unwanted tissue** (treatment).
Imaging needs radiation that **escapes** the body and is weakly ionising.
Treatment needs radiation that is **absorbed** by the tumour and damages its cells.
In both cases doctors try to keep the dose to healthy tissue as low as possible.

callouts.p: Medical uses are justified when the benefit (diagnosis or cure) outweighs the risk (cell damage, possible cancer later).

core.p: A **tracer** is a radioactive isotope, often attached to a chemical the body uses, that is injected, swallowed or inhaled. It travels to and collects in the organ being studied, and the radiation it emits is detected outside the body.
bullets: The tracer is usually a **gamma emitter**, for example **technetium-99m** (half-life about 6 hours).
A **gamma camera** outside the body detects the gamma rays and a computer builds an image.
Areas that absorb more tracer show up as **hot spots**; blocked or damaged areas absorb less.
Used to check, for example, kidney function, blood flow, bone or the thyroid gland.

callouts.p: A radioactive substance introduced into the body so that its path or location can be followed by detecting the radiation it emits.

core.h: Why tracers must be gamma emitters
core.p: The radiation has to get out of the body to reach the detector, and it should do as little damage as possible on the way.
bullets: **Gamma** is very penetrating, so it passes through tissue and out of the body.
Gamma is **weakly ionising**, so it causes less damage to cells it passes through.
**Alpha** would be absorbed within a few cells, so it could not be detected and would cause intense local damage.
**Beta** is partly absorbed by the body, so it is less suitable and gives a larger dose.

Ionisation

rows: No, stopped by a few cells

callouts.t: Do not say gamma is harmless
callouts.p: Gamma still ionises and can damage cells. Say it is weakly ionising and passes out of the body, so the dose is low.

core.h: Choosing the half-life of a tracer
core.p: The half-life must suit the time the procedure takes.
bullets: **Long enough** for the tracer to reach the organ and for the scan to be done before the activity falls too low.
**Short enough** that the patient does not stay radioactive for long, keeping the total dose small.
A few hours is ideal, which is why technetium-99m (about 6 hours) is widely used.
The tracer must also be **non-toxic** so it does not poison the patient chemically.

callouts.p: For a 2-mark 'why this half-life' question, give one reason it is not too short and one reason it is not too long.

core.p: Radiotherapy uses high doses of ionising radiation to damage the DNA of cancer cells so that they die or cannot divide. The aim is to give the tumour a large dose while sparing healthy tissue.
bullets: Ionising radiation damages DNA; cells that are badly damaged die.
Cancer cells divide rapidly, so they are particularly affected.
It can be done with an **external** source (beam from outside) or an **internal** source (inside the body).
The dose is carefully calculated and often split into several sessions to let healthy cells recover.

callouts.p: The use of ionising radiation to kill or control the growth of cancer cells.

core.p: High-energy **gamma rays** (or X-rays from a machine) are fired at the tumour from outside the body. The source or patient is rotated so beams come from several directions.
bullets: Gamma rays are used because they are **penetrating** enough to reach a tumour deep inside the body.
Several beams from different angles all **cross at the tumour**.
The tumour receives the **sum** of all beams, a very high dose.
Each region of healthy tissue receives only **one weak beam**, so it receives a lower dose.
Shielding (for example lead) protects other parts of the body and the staff.

callouts.p: Concentrates the dose on the tumour while spreading the dose to healthy tissue, so fewer healthy cells are killed.

bullets: Often uses a **beta emitter**, because beta is absorbed within a short distance of tissue.
Radiation is absorbed **locally** by the tumour, so nearby healthy tissue receives little.
Example: **iodine-131** is taken up by the thyroid gland and used to treat thyroid cancer or an overactive thyroid.
Small sealed **implants** (seeds or wires) can be put into a tumour and later removed or left to decay.
Alpha emitters are very ionising over a tiny range, so they can be used to kill cells very close to the source.

bullets: Imaging wants radiation to **leave** the body; treatment wants it **absorbed** by the tumour.
Imaging uses a **low dose**; treatment deliberately uses a **high dose** to the target.
Both prefer half-lives that do not leave the patient radioactive for longer than needed.

core.p: Because ionising radiation damages cells, all medical uses carry risk. Patients and staff are protected by keeping doses as low as possible.
bullets: Healthy cells near the tumour may be damaged or killed, causing side effects such as tiredness, sore skin, sickness or hair loss.
DNA damage in surviving cells can cause **mutations** and slightly raise the chance of a new cancer years later.
Patients with internal sources are temporarily radioactive, so contact with others may be limited for a short time.
Staff use **shielding**, **distance** and **short exposure time**, and wear dosimeters to monitor their dose.

callouts.p: A patient treated with an external gamma beam is irradiated, not contaminated, so they do not become radioactive. A patient given a tracer or iodine-131 is temporarily radioactive.

core.p: The spec asks you to **describe and evaluate** these uses. Evaluation means weighing advantages against disadvantages and reaching a judgement.
bullets: Advantage of tracers: see how organs are working **without surgery**, early diagnosis.
Disadvantage of tracers: small radiation dose, slight increase in cancer risk.
Advantage of radiotherapy: can cure or shrink cancers, sometimes without an operation.
Disadvantage of radiotherapy: damages healthy tissue, side effects, small risk of future cancer.
Judgement: usually justified because the risk from untreated disease is far greater than the radiation risk.

callouts.p: A 6-mark evaluation needs a clear conclusion that links the benefits and risks, not just two lists.

core.p: Doctors follow the principle of using the smallest dose that does the job.
bullets: Choose the right isotope: suitable radiation type and half-life.
Use the smallest activity that gives a clear image.
Aim treatment accurately using scans so beams hit only the tumour.
Split treatment into several sessions so healthy cells can repair between them.

core.p: Questions usually ask you to choose a suitable isotope, justify the radiation type or half-life, or evaluate a treatment.
bullets: Always link the property (penetration, ionisation, half-life) to the job.
Use the words **penetrating**, **ionising**, **absorbed** and **gamma camera**.
When given a table of isotopes, rule each one in or out with a reason.
Mention protecting healthy tissue whenever treatment is involved.

analogy.p: External radiotherapy is like several dim spotlights shining on one actor from different sides: each patch of stage they cross is only lightly lit, but where they all meet the actor is brilliantly lit. A tracer is like giving the actor a glowing badge so the audience can follow where they move without going on stage. The analogy breaks down because light does not damage the stage, whereas every ionising beam does some harm to the healthy tissue it passes through, and a radioactive tracer fades over time as it decays.

terms.d: A radioactive isotope put into the body so that its location can be followed by detecting its radiation.
A detector outside the body that detects gamma rays from a tracer and is used to build an image.
Using ionising radiation to kill or control cancer cells.
Treatment using beams of gamma rays (or X-rays) directed into the body from outside.
Treatment in which a radioactive source is placed inside the body near or in the tumour.
A mass of cells dividing out of control; it can be cancerous.
Able to remove electrons from atoms, which can damage cells and DNA.
How far radiation travels through materials before being absorbed.
High-frequency electromagnetic radiation from the nucleus; very penetrating, weakly ionising.
A high-speed electron emitted from the nucleus; moderately ionising, stopped by a few mm of aluminium.
Two protons and two neutrons (a helium nucleus); highly ionising, stopped by paper or skin.
The time for half the unstable nuclei in a sample to decay, or the activity to halve.
A gamma-emitting isotope with a half-life of about 6 hours, widely used as a medical tracer.
A beta-emitting isotope absorbed by the thyroid gland, used to treat thyroid conditions.
A measure of the harm caused by the radiation absorbed by the body, in sieverts (Sv).
A change in DNA that may be caused by ionising radiation and can lead to cancer.

mistakes.w: Alpha is used as a tracer because it is the most ionising.
mistakes.r: Alpha cannot be used as a tracer because it is absorbed inside the body and cannot reach the detector; it would also cause intense damage.

mistakes.w: Gamma is used for tracers because it is safe.
mistakes.r: Gamma is used because it is penetrating (escapes the body) and weakly ionising (less damage), not because it is harmless.

mistakes.w: The tracer should have a long half-life so it lasts.
mistakes.r: It needs a short half-life (a few hours): long enough to take the scan, short enough not to leave the patient radioactive.

mistakes.w: Radiotherapy uses one strong beam aimed at the tumour.
mistakes.r: Several weaker beams from different directions meet at the tumour, so healthy tissue gets a smaller dose.

mistakes.w: After radiotherapy the patient is radioactive.
mistakes.r: External beam treatment is irradiation, so the patient does not become radioactive.

mistakes.w: Radiation kills cancer cells but does not affect healthy cells.
mistakes.r: Radiation also damages healthy cells, so treatment is targeted and the dose to healthy tissue is minimised.

mistakes.w: The radiation shows up on an X-ray film.
mistakes.r: Gamma rays from the tracer are detected by a gamma camera outside the body and a computer forms the image.

mistakes.w: Tracers work because the radiation makes the organ glow.
mistakes.r: The tracer collects in the organ and emits gamma rays, which are detected; more tracer gives a stronger signal.

exam.q: State the type of radiation that should be emitted by a medical tracer.
model: Gamma.
exam.tip: One word answers are fine for 1 mark.

exam.q: Explain why an alpha emitter would not be suitable as a medical tracer.
model: Alpha is absorbed by the body / cannot pass out of the body to the detector.
Alpha is highly ionising so would damage cells / give a large dose.
exam.tip: Two marks: one about detection, one about harm.

exam.q: Technetium-99m has a half-life of 6 hours. Explain why this makes it suitable as a medical tracer.
model: Long enough for the tracer to travel to the organ and the scan to be taken.
Short enough that it decays quickly so the patient is not radioactive for long / lower dose.
exam.tip: Give both 'long enough' and 'short enough'.

exam.q: Describe how a radioactive tracer is used to check whether a patient's kidneys are working.
model: Gamma-emitting tracer injected (or swallowed) by the patient.
Tracer is carried in the blood and collects in / passes through the kidneys.
Gamma camera outside the body detects the gamma rays.
Image / count rate shows where tracer is; a kidney with less tracer or slow removal is not working properly.
exam.tip: Sequence: in, travels, detected, interpreted.

exam.q: In radiotherapy a tumour is targeted with gamma rays from several different directions. Explain why.
model: Beams all meet / overlap at the tumour, so it receives a high dose.
Each region of healthy tissue receives only one beam / a lower dose.
So fewer healthy cells are damaged / fewer side effects.
exam.tip: Mention both the tumour dose and the healthy tissue dose.

exam.q: Why are gamma rays used rather than beta particles for external radiotherapy of a deep tumour?
model: Gamma is penetrating / can pass through tissue to reach a deep tumour.
Beta would be absorbed by the skin / tissue near the surface.
exam.tip: Link penetrating power to the depth of the tumour.

exam.q: Iodine-131 is a beta emitter absorbed by the thyroid gland. Explain why it is used to treat thyroid cancer.
model: Iodine is taken up / concentrated by the thyroid.
Beta is ionising and damages / kills the cancer cells.
Beta has a short range in tissue so is absorbed locally / little damage to other organs.
exam.tip: Say why the isotope goes to the right place AND why beta suits treatment.

exam.q: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of using a radioactive tracer for diagnosis.
model: Advantage: shows how an organ is working without surgery / early diagnosis.
Disadvantage: patient receives a dose of ionising radiation / small increased risk of cancer.
exam.tip: Be specific about the type of risk.

exam.q: A patient is given a tracer. Suggest one precaution the patient might take for a day afterwards and explain why.
model: Avoid close contact with young children / pregnant women.
Patient is temporarily radioactive and emits gamma, which could irradiate others.
exam.tip: Link the precaution to the patient being a source.

exam.q: Evaluate the use of nuclear radiation in medicine for diagnosing and treating cancer.
model: Tracers (gamma, short half-life) collect in organs and are detected by a gamma camera.
Allows diagnosis without surgery, low dose because gamma weakly ionising and short half-life.
Radiotherapy kills cancer cells by ionisation damaging DNA.
External gamma beams from several directions concentrate dose on tumour; internal beta sources are absorbed locally.
Risks: healthy cells damaged, side effects, mutations that may cause cancer later; staff exposure reduced by shielding and distance.
Justified conclusion: benefits usually outweigh the small risks when doses are kept as low as possible.
exam.tip: Describe both uses, give pros and cons of each, and finish with a judgement.

worked.q: A hospital can choose from these isotopes for a liver scan: P (alpha, 4 hours), Q (gamma, 6 hours), R (gamma, 30 years), S (beta, 8 days). Which should it choose? Justify your choice.
steps: Rule out P: alpha would not leave the body to reach the gamma camera and is highly ionising.
Rule out S: beta is partly absorbed by the body, giving a larger dose and a poorer image, and 8 days is longer than needed.
Rule out R: gamma is right but a 30 year half-life would leave the patient radioactive for years.
Q is gamma (escapes the body, weakly ionising) and its 6 hour half-life is long enough for the scan but short enough to decay quickly.

worked.q: A tracer with a half-life of 6 hours has an activity of 400 MBq when injected. What is its activity 24 hours later, and why does this matter for the patient?
steps: Number of half-lives = 24 / 6 = 4.
Activity after 24 hours is 25 MBq, 1/16 of the starting value.
worked.ans: 25 MBq. Within a day the patient's activity has fallen to a small fraction, so their total dose and the risk to people around them are low.

worked.q: Model answer: Explain how external radiotherapy destroys a tumour while limiting damage to healthy tissue.
steps: A source of gamma rays (penetrating enough to reach deep tumours) is used.
The beam is aimed at the tumour from several different directions, for example by rotating the source around the patient.
All the beams overlap at the tumour, so it receives a high total dose; ionisation damages the DNA of cancer cells and kills them.
Healthy tissue along each path receives only one beam, so it gets a much smaller dose; lead shielding protects the rest of the body.
Treatment is split into several sessions so that healthy cells can repair between doses.
worked.ans: The tumour gets a high combined dose and is destroyed, while each part of healthy tissue receives only a small dose.

phy_ocra.15.3.summary: **Nuclear fission** is the splitting of a large, unstable nucleus such as **uranium-235** into two smaller **daughter nuclei**, releasing two or three **neutrons**, **gamma radiation** and a large amount of energy, mostly as the **kinetic energy** of the fragments. Fission is usually triggered when the nucleus absorbs a neutron, and because each fission releases more neutrons, these can cause further fissions in a **chain reaction**. In a nuclear reactor the chain reaction is **controlled** with control rods and a moderator so that energy is released at a steady rate; in a nuclear bomb it is uncontrolled. The fission products are themselves radioactive, which links fission to the problem of nuclear waste.

core.p: Some very large nuclei are unstable. As well as decaying by alpha, beta or gamma emission, a very heavy nucleus can **split into two smaller nuclei**. This is fission.
bullets: Heavy nuclei such as **uranium-235** and **plutonium-239** can undergo fission.
Fission can happen **spontaneously**, but this is rare.
Usually fission is **induced**: the nucleus first **absorbs a neutron**, which makes it even more unstable.
The two smaller nuclei are called **daughter nuclei** or **fission products**.

callouts.p: The splitting of a large, unstable nucleus into two smaller nuclei, with the release of neutrons, radiation and energy.

core.p: For uranium-235 the process follows a clear sequence that examiners expect in order.
bullets: A **slow (thermal) neutron** is absorbed by a uranium-235 nucleus.
It becomes **uranium-236**, which is very unstable.
The U-236 nucleus **splits** into two smaller daughter nuclei of roughly similar size (for example barium and krypton).
**Two or three neutrons** are released, together with **gamma rays**.
A large amount of energy is released, mostly as **kinetic energy** of the daughter nuclei and neutrons.

fig.cap: Induced fission: a slow neutron is absorbed by uranium-235, forming unstable uranium-236, which splits into barium-141 and krypton-92 and releases three neutrons, gamma radiation and energy.

core.p: Fission can be written as a nuclear equation. As in all nuclear equations, the **mass numbers** (top) and **atomic numbers** (bottom) must balance on each side.
bullets: Example: U-235 (92 protons) + 1 neutron -> Ba-141 (56 protons) + Kr-92 (36 protons) + 3 neutrons.
Mass numbers: 235 + 1 = 236 and 141 + 92 + 3 = 236, balanced.
Atomic numbers: 92 + 0 = 92 and 56 + 36 + 0 = 92, balanced.
A neutron is written with mass number 1 and atomic number 0.
Different fissions of U-235 give different pairs of daughter nuclei; the numbers always balance.

callouts.p: Subtract the known mass numbers from the total to find the missing mass number, and do the same with atomic numbers. Then use the atomic number to name the element if a periodic table is given.

core.p: The spec asks you to relate fission to the **transfer of energy to other particles**. The energy released by the nucleus does not stay in the nucleus.
bullets: Most energy is carried as **kinetic energy** of the fast-moving daughter nuclei.
The neutrons also leave with kinetic energy.
Some energy leaves as **gamma radiation**.
The fast fragments collide with surrounding atoms, sharing their kinetic energy, so the fuel gets **hot** (thermal energy store increases).
In a power station this thermal energy heats a coolant, makes steam and drives turbines and generators.

callouts.p: One fission releases millions of times more energy than a chemical reaction such as burning one molecule of fuel, which is why a small mass of uranium releases so much energy.

core.p: Fission is accompanied by several kinds of radiation, which is why reactors need heavy shielding.
bullets: **Neutrons** are released directly in each fission.
**Gamma rays** are emitted when fission occurs.
The daughter nuclei usually have too many neutrons, so they are **radioactive** and later decay, mostly by **beta** and gamma emission.
This is why spent fuel is highly radioactive waste.
Thick concrete and steel shielding absorb the neutrons and gamma rays.

callouts.p: In alpha decay a nucleus emits a small alpha particle. In fission it splits into two large nuclei of similar size plus neutrons. Do not mix these up.

core.p: Each fission releases two or three neutrons. If at least one of these is absorbed by another uranium-235 nucleus, that nucleus splits too, releasing more neutrons. The process can keep itself going.
bullets: One fission -> 2 or 3 neutrons -> more fissions -> more neutrons.
If on average more than one neutron per fission causes another fission, the reaction rate **grows rapidly**.
If on average exactly one neutron per fission causes another fission, the reaction proceeds at a **steady rate**.
If fewer than one does, the reaction **dies out**.
Neutrons can be lost by escaping from the fuel or being absorbed by other materials.

callouts.p: A reaction in which the neutrons released by one fission go on to cause further fissions, so the process is self-sustaining.

fig.cap: A chain reaction: neutrons from each fission (green circles are uranium-235 nuclei splitting) go on to split more nuclei, so the number of fissions can double with each generation if it is not controlled.

core.p: The same chain reaction can release energy safely or explosively, depending on how many neutrons go on to cause further fissions.
bullets: **Controlled**: one neutron per fission, on average, causes another fission; steady energy output in a **nuclear reactor**.
**Uncontrolled**: the number of fissions rises extremely quickly; huge energy release in a very short time in a **nuclear weapon**.
There must be enough fissile material close together (a large enough mass) for a chain reaction to keep going, otherwise too many neutrons escape.

core.p: A reactor is designed to keep the chain reaction steady and transfer the thermal energy safely to a generator.
bullets: **Fuel rods** contain uranium (enriched in U-235).
The **moderator** (for example graphite or water) slows down fast neutrons so they are more likely to be absorbed by U-235 and cause fission.
**Control rods** (for example boron) **absorb neutrons**; lowering them in slows the reaction, raising them speeds it up.
The **coolant** (water or gas) carries thermal energy away to a heat exchanger to make steam.
Steam drives a turbine, which turns a generator.
Thick **concrete shielding** absorbs neutrons and gamma radiation.

callouts.p: The moderator slows neutrons down (helping fission). Control rods absorb neutrons (reducing fission). Students often swap them.

core.p: Neutrons released by fission are moving very fast. U-235 is much more likely to absorb a slow neutron than a fast one.
bullets: Fast neutrons tend to pass through or bounce off nuclei without being absorbed.
The moderator slows them by collisions with its atoms, transferring kinetic energy to the moderator.
Slowed (thermal) neutrons are readily absorbed by U-235, keeping the chain reaction going.

core.h: Benefits and drawbacks of fission power
core.p: You may be asked to weigh up nuclear fission as an energy resource.
bullets: Advantage: very large energy from a small mass of fuel.
Advantage: no carbon dioxide released during generation, so does not add to global warming while running.
Advantage: reliable, steady output not dependent on weather.
Disadvantage: produces **radioactive waste**, some with long half-lives, needing long-term storage.
Disadvantage: risk of accidents releasing radioactive material; expensive to build and decommission.
Uranium is a **non-renewable** resource.

core.p: Fission obeys the same conservation rules as other nuclear changes.
bullets: Total mass number (nucleons) is conserved.
Total atomic number (charge) is conserved.
Energy is conserved: energy from the nucleus is transferred to kinetic energy of the products and to radiation.
The total mass of the products is very slightly less than the starting mass; this is linked to the energy released.

core.p: Fission questions commonly ask you to describe the process, complete an equation, or explain how a reactor controls the chain reaction.
bullets: Use the key sequence: **neutron absorbed -> nucleus unstable -> splits into two daughter nuclei -> 2 or 3 neutrons + gamma + energy**.
For chain reactions say that the released neutrons **go on to be absorbed** by other nuclei and **cause further fissions**.
For control rods use the phrase **absorb neutrons**.
For energy say **kinetic energy** of the products, which heats the surroundings.

analogy.t: Falling dominoes that set off more dominoes
analogy.p: A chain reaction is like a domino layout where each domino that falls knocks over two or three others, so the toppling spreads faster and faster. Control rods are like removing some dominoes so that each fall knocks over only one more, giving a steady line of falls instead of an avalanche. The analogy breaks down because dominoes always hit the next one, whereas neutrons move randomly and many escape or are absorbed without causing fission, and a falling domino does not release extra energy in the way a splitting nucleus does.

terms.d: The splitting of a large unstable nucleus into two smaller nuclei, releasing neutrons, radiation and energy.
Fission caused by a nucleus absorbing a neutron.
Fission that happens without a neutron being absorbed; rare.
The two smaller nuclei produced when a large nucleus splits; also called fission products.
A self-sustaining process in which neutrons released by fission cause further fissions.
The isotope of uranium that undergoes fission when it absorbs a slow neutron; used as reactor fuel.
An uncharged particle in the nucleus; released during fission and able to trigger further fissions.
Material (such as graphite or water) that slows down fast neutrons so they are more likely to cause fission.
Rods (for example of boron) that absorb neutrons to control the rate of the chain reaction.
A fluid that carries thermal energy away from the reactor core.
Energy of a moving object; most fission energy is carried as kinetic energy of the fragments.
High-frequency electromagnetic radiation emitted from the nucleus during fission.
The total number of protons and neutrons in a nucleus.
The number of protons in a nucleus.
Thick material such as concrete that absorbs neutrons and gamma rays around a reactor.

mistakes.w: Fission is when two nuclei join together.
mistakes.r: Fission is splitting one large nucleus into two smaller ones; joining is fusion.

mistakes.w: The uranium atom splits.
mistakes.r: It is the nucleus that splits; use the word nucleus.

mistakes.w: Uranium splits into two halves and releases electrons.
mistakes.r: It splits into two smaller daughter nuclei (not usually equal) and releases 2 or 3 neutrons plus gamma rays.

mistakes.w: Control rods slow down the neutrons.
mistakes.r: Control rods absorb neutrons; the moderator slows them down.

mistakes.w: A chain reaction is when one atom decays after another.
mistakes.r: A chain reaction is when neutrons released from one fission are absorbed by other nuclei and cause further fissions.

mistakes.w: Energy is released as heat directly from the nucleus.
mistakes.r: Energy is released mainly as kinetic energy of the fission products, which then heats the surroundings through collisions.

mistakes.w: Fission products are stable and harmless.
mistakes.r: Fission products are usually radioactive, which is why spent fuel is dangerous waste.

mistakes.w: In a bomb fewer neutrons are released.
mistakes.r: Each fission releases the same 2 or 3 neutrons; in a bomb more of them go on to cause fission, so the reaction is uncontrolled.

exam.q: What is meant by nuclear fission?
model: A large (unstable) nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei.
exam.tip: Use the word nucleus, not atom.

exam.q: Describe what happens when a uranium-235 nucleus undergoes induced fission.
model: Nucleus absorbs a (slow) neutron.
Becomes unstable (U-236).
Splits into two smaller (daughter) nuclei.
Releases 2 or 3 neutrons and energy / gamma radiation.
exam.tip: Four marks: four steps in order.

exam.q: Complete the equation: U-235 + neutron -> Ba-144 + Kr-? + 2 neutrons. (Ba has 56 protons, U has 92.)
model: Mass number: 236 - 144 - 2 = 90.
Atomic number: 92 - 56 = 36, so Kr-90 with 36 protons.
exam.tip: Remember neutrons count 1 each to the mass number and 0 to the atomic number.

exam.q: Explain how a chain reaction occurs in uranium fuel.
model: Each fission releases 2 or 3 neutrons.
These neutrons are absorbed by other U-235 nuclei.
Which then undergo fission and release more neutrons, so the process continues.
exam.tip: Mention the neutrons explicitly, they drive the chain.

exam.q: State the function of the control rods in a nuclear reactor.
model: Absorb neutrons (to control the rate of fission).
exam.tip: The key word is absorb.

exam.q: Explain why a moderator is needed in a nuclear reactor.
model: Slows down neutrons released by fission.
Slow neutrons are more likely to be absorbed by U-235 / cause fission.
exam.tip: Link slowing to absorption.

exam.q: Describe how energy released in fission ends up heating the water in a reactor.
model: Energy released as kinetic energy of the fission products / neutrons.
Fragments collide with surrounding atoms and transfer energy.
Fuel and coolant temperature increase; coolant carries energy to heat water / make steam.
exam.tip: Use energy-store language: kinetic to thermal.

exam.q: Explain the difference between the chain reaction in a nuclear reactor and in a nuclear bomb.
model: Reactor: controlled, on average one neutron per fission causes another fission, steady energy release.
Bomb: uncontrolled, more than one neutron per fission causes fission so energy released almost instantly.
exam.tip: Compare directly using 'whereas'.

exam.q: Explain why the spent fuel from a reactor is radioactive even though uranium-235 has been used up.
model: Fission products / daughter nuclei are unstable / have too many neutrons.
They decay, emitting beta and gamma radiation.
exam.tip: Fission products, not uranium, are the main source of activity.

exam.q: Describe how a nuclear reactor uses fission to produce a steady output of energy and explain how the operators would respond if the reaction rate began to increase.
model: U-235 absorbs a slow neutron, splits into two daughter nuclei, releasing 2-3 neutrons and energy.
Neutrons cause further fissions in a chain reaction.
Moderator slows neutrons so they can be absorbed and cause fission.
Control rods absorb neutrons so on average one neutron per fission causes another, giving a steady rate.
Coolant removes thermal energy to make steam which drives turbines and generators.
If rate increases, control rods are lowered further to absorb more neutrons, reducing the number of fissions.
exam.tip: Cover process, chain reaction, control and energy transfer, then answer the 'respond' part explicitly.

worked.q: Plutonium-239 (94 protons) absorbs a neutron and splits into xenon-134 (54 protons), another nucleus X and 3 neutrons. Find the mass number and atomic number of X.
steps: Total mass number on the left = 239 + 1 = 240.
Mass number of X = 240 - 134 - 3 = 103.
Total atomic number on the left = 94 + 0 = 94.
Atomic number of X = 94 - 54 - 0 = 40.
worked.ans: X has mass number 103 and atomic number 40 (zirconium-103).

worked.q: In a chain reaction each fission releases 2 neutrons and both cause further fissions. How many fissions happen in the 5th generation if the first generation is a single fission?
steps: Generation 1: 1 fission.
Generation 2: 2 fissions; generation 3: 4; generation 4: 8.
Generation 5: 16 fissions.
In general, generation n has 2^(n-1) fissions.
worked.ans: 16 fissions. This doubling is why an uncontrolled chain reaction releases energy explosively, and why control rods must absorb the extra neutrons in a reactor.

worked.q: Model answer: A reactor is running at a steady rate. Explain what happens if the control rods are raised out of the core.
steps: Control rods absorb neutrons.
Raising them means fewer neutrons are absorbed by the rods.
More neutrons are available to be absorbed by U-235 nuclei, so on average more than one neutron per fission causes another fission.
The rate of fission increases, so energy is released faster and the core temperature rises.
worked.ans: The chain reaction speeds up and the power output (and temperature) rises; the rods must be lowered again to restore a steady rate.

phy_ocra.15.4.summary: **Nuclear fusion** is the joining of two light nuclei, such as isotopes of hydrogen, to form a heavier nucleus, releasing a large amount of energy. Fusion of **hydrogen into helium** is the energy source of the **Sun and other stars**, where enormous temperatures and pressures force nuclei together. Fusion is very hard to achieve on Earth because all nuclei are **positively charged** and **repel** each other, so they must be heated to over 100 million degrees to move fast enough to get close enough to fuse, and the resulting **plasma** must be contained without touching any material. If it can be made practical, fusion would offer abundant fuel, no carbon dioxide and far less long-lived radioactive waste than fission.

core.p: In fusion, two **light nuclei** join (fuse) to make a single heavier nucleus. It is the opposite of fission, where a heavy nucleus splits.
bullets: Typical fuels are isotopes of hydrogen: **deuterium** (H-2, 1 proton and 1 neutron) and **tritium** (H-3, 1 proton and 2 neutrons).
The product is usually **helium**, often with a free neutron.
Fusion releases a large amount of energy per kilogram of fuel, even more than fission.
The products have slightly less total mass than the reactants; this mass difference corresponds to the energy released.

callouts.p: The joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus, with the release of energy.

core.p: The reaction most studied for fusion power on Earth is deuterium plus tritium.
bullets: H-2 + H-3 -> He-4 + neutron + energy.
Mass numbers: 2 + 3 = 5 and 4 + 1 = 5, balanced.
Atomic numbers: 1 + 1 = 2 and 2 + 0 = 2, balanced.
Most of the energy is carried away as **kinetic energy** of the fast neutron and helium nucleus.

callouts.p: Fusion equations are checked exactly like fission and decay equations: top numbers (mass) and bottom numbers (atomic) must both balance.

core.p: Stars, including the Sun, are powered by fusion. In the core, hydrogen nuclei fuse, in several steps, to make helium.
bullets: The core of the Sun is at about **15 million degrees** and at enormous pressure and density.
**Gravity** squeezes the core, keeping it hot and dense so that nuclei collide often enough to fuse.
Energy released by fusion is transferred outwards and radiated from the surface as light and other electromagnetic radiation.
The outward pressure from fusion energy balances the inward pull of gravity, keeping the star stable for most of its life.
Fusion in stars also creates heavier elements over the star's life.

callouts.p: The fusion of hydrogen nuclei to form helium is the source of energy for stars.

core.h: Why fusion is difficult: electrostatic repulsion
core.p: Nuclei contain protons, so every nucleus is **positively charged**. Like charges **repel**, and this repulsion gets stronger the closer they get.
bullets: For fusion, nuclei must come **extremely close** together, so that the strong nuclear force (which only acts over tiny distances) can pull them together.
To get that close they must overcome the **electrostatic repulsion** between them.
This needs nuclei moving at **very high speeds**, which means a **very high temperature** (high kinetic energy of particles).
A high **density** (pressure) is also needed so that collisions happen often enough.

callouts.p: The repulsion that stops fusion is between the positive nuclei, not between electrons. At fusion temperatures the electrons have been stripped off.

core.p: At the temperatures needed for fusion, atoms lose their electrons completely, forming a **plasma**: a hot gas of nuclei and free electrons.
bullets: Fusion reactors on Earth need temperatures of over **100 million degrees**, hotter than the Sun's core, because they cannot match the Sun's huge pressure.
No material container can survive touching a plasma this hot.
Because the plasma is made of charged particles, it can be held in place by **strong magnetic fields**.

core.p: Scientists have built experimental fusion reactors, but none yet produces useful electricity.
bullets: A **tokamak** is a doughnut-shaped vessel in which strong **magnetic fields** hold the plasma away from the walls.
The plasma is heated by electric currents, microwaves and particle beams.
Another approach uses powerful lasers to heat and squeeze tiny fuel pellets.
So far, experiments have produced fusion, but it is very hard to get **more energy out than is put in** for long enough to be practical.
Large international projects are working to build reactors that release more energy than they use.

core.h: Difficulties of achieving fusion on Earth
core.p: Examiners like a clear list of the problems and why each one matters.
bullets: Very **high temperature** needed to overcome repulsion between positive nuclei.
High **pressure or density** needed so that collisions are frequent.
The plasma must be **contained** without touching the walls, which would cool it and damage the vessel.
It takes a great deal of energy to heat and contain the plasma, so getting a **net energy gain** is very hard.
Tritium is rare and radioactive, so it must be produced.
Building and running reactors is very **expensive**.

callouts.p: For 'explain why fusion is difficult' always link the high temperature to the need to overcome electrostatic repulsion between positively charged nuclei.

core.p: Both release energy from nuclei, but in opposite ways, with different fuels and waste.
bullets: Fission splits heavy nuclei; fusion joins light nuclei.
Fission is used in power stations now; fusion power is still experimental.
Fusion fuel is plentiful; fission fuel (uranium) is limited.

core.p: Fusion is attractive because of its fuel and its waste.
bullets: **Deuterium** can be extracted from seawater, so fuel is plentiful.
No carbon dioxide is released, so it does not contribute to global warming.
The main product, **helium**, is not radioactive.
Produces much less long-lived radioactive waste than fission (reactor parts become radioactive from neutrons, but mostly with shorter half-lives).
If the plasma is disturbed it cools and fusion simply stops, so there is no runaway chain reaction.

core.p: Where does the energy come from? The nuclei after fusion are more tightly bound, and their total mass is very slightly less than the mass of the original nuclei.
bullets: The small loss of mass corresponds to the energy released.
Per kilogram of fuel, fusion releases several times more energy than fission and millions of times more than burning fossil fuels.
Only light nuclei release energy by fusing; very heavy nuclei release energy by splitting instead.

callouts.t: Mass is not destroyed by magic
callouts.p: Do not write that mass 'turns into heat'. Say the products have slightly less mass and the corresponding energy is released, mainly as kinetic energy of the products.

core.p: Fusion questions are usually short recall or explain questions, plus comparisons with fission.
bullets: Definition: two light nuclei **join** to form a heavier nucleus and release energy.
Stars: **hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium**.
Difficulty: nuclei are **positive** so **repel**; need **very high temperature** (and pressure) so they move fast enough to get close enough to fuse.
Containment: plasma held by **magnetic fields**.
Always use the word **nuclei**, not atoms.

analogy.p: Fusing two nuclei is like trying to push the north poles of two strong magnets together: the closer they get, the harder they push apart, so you have to throw them at each other very fast. If you get them close enough, a much stronger short-range glue (the strong nuclear force) suddenly snaps them together and releases energy. The analogy breaks down because magnets repel through magnetism, whereas nuclei repel because of their positive electric charge, and pushing magnets together does not release energy.

terms.d: The joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy.
An isotope of hydrogen with 1 proton and 1 neutron (H-2).
A radioactive isotope of hydrogen with 1 proton and 2 neutrons (H-3).
Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
The force pushing apart two objects with the same type of charge, such as two positive nuclei.
A very strong attractive force between nucleons that acts only over very short distances.
A very hot state of matter in which atoms have lost their electrons, leaving nuclei and free electrons.
A doughnut-shaped fusion reactor that uses magnetic fields to contain a hot plasma.
Using strong magnetic fields to hold a plasma away from the walls of its container.
The very hot, dense centre of a star where hydrogen fusion takes place.
A nucleus with 2 protons and 2 neutrons; the main product of hydrogen fusion.
Energy of motion; higher temperature means particles have more kinetic energy.
Getting more energy out of a reactor than is put in to run it.
The splitting of a heavy nucleus into two smaller nuclei, releasing energy.

mistakes.w: Fusion is when a nucleus splits.
mistakes.r: Fusion is the joining of two light nuclei; splitting is fission.

mistakes.w: Two atoms join together.
mistakes.r: Two nuclei join together; at fusion temperatures the electrons have been stripped away.

mistakes.w: High temperature is needed to melt the hydrogen.
mistakes.r: High temperature gives nuclei enough kinetic energy (speed) to overcome the electrostatic repulsion between positive nuclei.

mistakes.w: The nuclei repel because their electrons repel.
mistakes.r: The nuclei repel because they are both positively charged (protons).

mistakes.w: The Sun burns hydrogen.
mistakes.r: The Sun fuses hydrogen nuclei to form helium; it is a nuclear process, not chemical burning.

mistakes.w: Fusion power stations already supply electricity.
mistakes.r: Fusion has been achieved in experiments, but no reactor yet produces useful electrical power on a commercial scale.

mistakes.w: Fusion produces lots of long-lived radioactive waste, like fission.
mistakes.r: Fusion produces helium (not radioactive) and much less long-lived waste than fission.

mistakes.w: The plasma is held in a strong steel container.
mistakes.r: It is held by magnetic fields, because any solid container would be damaged and would cool the plasma.

exam.q: What is nuclear fusion?
model: Two light nuclei join to form a heavier nucleus (releasing energy).
exam.tip: Use 'nuclei', not 'atoms'.

exam.q: State the source of energy in stars.
model: Fusion of hydrogen nuclei (to form helium).
exam.tip: Name both the process and the fuel.

exam.q: Complete the equation: H-2 + H-3 -> He-? + neutron.
model: He-4 (mass number 4, atomic number 2).
exam.tip: Total mass number on the left is 5; the neutron takes 1.

exam.q: Explain why fusion only happens at very high temperatures.
model: Nuclei are positively charged so they repel each other.
High temperature means nuclei have high kinetic energy / move very fast.
So they can overcome the repulsion and get close enough to fuse.
exam.tip: Charge, speed, closeness: three marks.

exam.q: Explain why the plasma in a fusion reactor must not touch the walls of the reactor.
model: Plasma would cool down so fusion would stop.
Walls would be damaged / melted by the extremely high temperature.
exam.tip: Give a reason linked to the plasma and one linked to the walls.

exam.q: Describe how the plasma is kept away from the walls of a tokamak.
model: Strong magnetic fields are used.
Plasma is made of charged particles which are affected by / held by the magnetic field.
exam.tip: Link magnetic fields to charged particles.

exam.q: Suggest two advantages of fusion over fission as a source of energy.
model: Fuel is plentiful (deuterium from seawater).
Much less long-lived radioactive waste / helium product not radioactive / no runaway chain reaction.
exam.tip: Any two distinct advantages.

exam.q: Explain why fusion happens naturally in the core of the Sun but is difficult to achieve on Earth.
model: Sun's core has extremely high temperature and pressure/density due to gravity.
So nuclei move fast enough and collide often enough to overcome repulsion and fuse.
On Earth we cannot create the Sun's pressure, so even higher temperatures (over 100 million degrees) are needed.
Hard to contain plasma / need more energy in than is easily got out.
exam.tip: Contrast conditions in the Sun with what we can do on Earth.

exam.q: Compare nuclear fission and nuclear fusion.
model: Fission: heavy nucleus splits; fusion: light nuclei join.
Fission fuel uranium/plutonium; fusion fuel hydrogen isotopes.
Fission needs a neutron to be absorbed; fusion needs very high temperature and pressure.
Fission produces long-lived radioactive waste; fusion produces much less / helium. Both release large amounts of energy.
exam.tip: Each mark needs a direct comparison, not two separate descriptions.

exam.q: Scientists are spending large amounts of money trying to build fusion power stations. Discuss the benefits of fusion power and the problems that must be solved.
model: Fusion joins light nuclei (deuterium and tritium) to make helium, releasing large amounts of energy per kg.
Benefit: deuterium plentiful from seawater, so fuel will not run out quickly.
Benefit: no carbon dioxide, much less long-lived radioactive waste, no runaway chain reaction.
Problem: positive nuclei repel, so temperatures over 100 million degrees are needed.
Problem: plasma must be contained by magnetic fields without touching walls; hard to sustain.
Problem: so far hard to get more energy out than is put in; very expensive; conclusion that benefits may justify the cost.
exam.tip: Balance benefits and problems and finish with a short judgement.

worked.q: Two deuterium nuclei (H-2) fuse to form a nucleus X and a neutron. Find X.
steps: Total mass number on the left = 2 + 2 = 4.
Mass number of X = 4 - 1 = 3.
Total atomic number on the left = 1 + 1 = 2.
Atomic number of X = 2 - 0 = 2, so X is helium.
worked.ans: X is helium-3 (mass number 3, atomic number 2).

worked.q: Model answer: Explain why fusion needs both a very high temperature and a high density.
steps: Nuclei are positively charged and repel each other more strongly as they get closer.
A very high temperature gives the nuclei very high kinetic energy, so some can get close enough for the strong nuclear force to pull them together.
A high density means there are many nuclei in a small space, so collisions happen often.
Both are needed so that enough fusions happen every second to release useful amounts of energy.
worked.ans: High temperature lets nuclei overcome electrostatic repulsion; high density makes such collisions frequent enough for useful energy output.

worked.q: Applied example: A student says 'the Sun gets its energy the same way as a nuclear power station'. Correct the statement.
steps: A nuclear power station uses fission: heavy uranium-235 nuclei split after absorbing neutrons.
The Sun uses fusion: light hydrogen nuclei join to form helium in its very hot, dense core.
Both release energy from nuclei, but by opposite processes.
worked.ans: The statement is wrong: the Sun releases energy by nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium, whereas power stations release energy by nuclear fission of uranium.
